record_identity.title: Compromised Mistral SDK package executed credential-harvesting payload on import

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Mini Shai-Hulud / TanStack compromise affecting Mistral SDK releases
incident_identity.date_basis: Mistral states compromised npm packages were uploaded on 11 May 2026 and the compromised PyPI release on 12 May 2026; affected releases were removed within hours.

summary: Mistral reported that the Mini Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack on TanStack resulted in compromised Mistral npm and PyPI SDK versions being published. The compromised PyPI package `mistralai==2.4.6` executed malicious code when client modules were imported on Linux, downloading a background payload that harvested credentials from common locations. Mistral reported no impact to its global infrastructure and removed the affected releases. Its updated advisory says the compromised npm releases referenced a missing file, preventing their malicious path from running. The working PyPI payload was Linux-specific. Mistral later marked mitigation and closed its investigation. The repository advisory distinguishes client-module imports from a bare namespace import. It also records quarantine of the Python project.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Mistral's security advisory identifies affected npm and PyPI versions, publication windows and indicators of compromise. It states that the compromised PyPI release executed a malicious script on Linux at import time and launched a detached process designed to harvest credentials. Aikido Security separately reports that its malware team detected compromised npm package versions including @mistralai releases in the wider campaign. Its account documents external post-publication detection, not the exact Mistral internal monitoring control or the causal route to removal. The updated advisory distinguishes nonfunctional npm payload paths from the working Linux PyPI import path. Investigation closure on 14 May does not prove downstream customer cleanup or absence of credential exposure. The repository security advisory supplies additional direct evidence for the Python release. It reports no corresponding repository release lineage and an upload outside the normal release pipeline. It identifies the client-module import trigger and records quarantine. These facts support separate conclusions about attributed origin and containment without joining the external detection and provider response into one internal mechanism.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The compromised Python release represented attacker content under the Mistral SDK identity without matching legitimate release lineage. Its source attribution is Not aligned. The release withdrawal and Python-project quarantine are Aligned for the bounded purpose of containing further distribution through the affected channel. The external detection and provider response remain causally distinct in the available accounts. No particular pre-publication safeguard is presumed to have failed. The malicious executable asset also presents a software-integrity property beyond the origin-attribution and response findings. The selectable taxonomy does not fully represent that property without additional evidence of an authority-conversion mechanism. The nonfunctional npm path remains distinct from the working Linux Python path. Customer cleanup and credential exposure remain unknown. The independent AI software-security and repair assessments are preserved. Harm Impact: The publisher confirms actual malicious SDK versions were released through its distribution channel. Those persisted releases changed the expected integrity of a real software asset, establishing the S2 integrity minimum. Customer restoration burden remains unknown. The Mistral advisory identifies unauthorised compromised SDK releases and a Python upload outside the normal release lineage. Package contents were changed through the trusted distribution surface. Public package readability does not authorise an unrelated party to replace its release content. No unobserved victim-secret exfiltration is inferred.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: AI-system governance includes the developer infrastructure surrounding a model. Compromised package provenance can expose credentials and downstream systems before the model is ever invoked, making third-party build dependencies, release integrity and incident response part of the assurance boundary.
assessment_boundaries: Mistral reports no impact to its global infrastructure.
The npm packages were compromised but Mistral reports their malicious code path was non-functional; the PyPI package did execute a credential-harvesting payload.
The public advisory does not quantify how many customers installed or executed the affected PyPI release or whether credentials were successfully exfiltrated from customer systems.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Mistral says the TanStack worm compromised a developer device and led to malicious SDK releases. Its investigation found no impact to global infrastructure.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: The developer-device pathway must remain distinct from global compromise.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Compromised npm SDK versions were published on 11 May and removed early on 12 May. PyPI mistralai 2.4.6 was published and removed on 12 May. Trusted package identities carried attacker content.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Package provenance substitution and payload execution are different questions.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The malicious Python release used the Mistral SDK package identity. The repository advisory identifies no matching release tag, commit or workflow and says the upload bypassed the normal publishing pipeline. The attributed package origin therefore differed materially from the supported contribution history. This affected developer trust and reuse. A genuine distribution endpoint does not make the attacker’s contribution an authorised Mistral release. This finding is bounded to that Python release; valid workflow provenance elsewhere in the campaign does not prove code safety or establish the same publishing route here.

Compromised SDK versions were published through a trusted release identity outside the normal release lineage. Publication changed the protected package contents. This is distinct from whether a victim later executed credential harvesting.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The PyPI version ran malicious code on Linux import and launched a detached credential-harvesting process. The repository advisory specifies imports under mistralai.client on Linux; a bare namespace import does not trigger the loader.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Reported payload behaviour does not quantify actual stolen credentials.

clauses.source_paraphrase: The updated advisory says the compromised npm releases referenced a missing file, so their malicious path could not run. It still instructed users to remove them.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A compromised release is distinct from a working payload.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Aikido separately detected malicious npm versions. Mistral removed its affected releases within hours, but the public accounts do not link one operative Mistral control to detection and withdrawal. The repository advisory also records quarantine of the Python project. That protective action can be assessed separately from the causal route connecting the external detection to provider withdrawal.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: External detection and provider removal must retain their separate causal limits.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: Mistral withdrew the compromised SDK versions within hours. The Python project was also quarantined. These measures acted on the identified malicious distribution and limited further availability through the affected release channel. This establishes a bounded protective effect for release containment. It does not establish customer credential recovery, removal from private caches or the effectiveness of every earlier safeguard. Aikido’s detection need not be proved to have caused Mistral’s action to assess the withdrawal itself.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Mistral marked mitigation on 13 May and closed its investigation on 14 May. It advised affected users to clean systems, rotate accessible secrets and review cloud logs and retained package copies.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Advised downstream remediation is distinct from confirmed completion at every customer.

source_clause_analysis.purpose: Present source-backed material actions and later responses in supported relative order. Separate runs, source attributions and unknown ordering remain explicit.

external_assessments.assessment_title: TanStack supply chain attack affecting Mistral SDK packages
external_assessments.scope_note: The security advisory diagnoses the same software-supply-chain occurrence but does not quantify customer execution or successful credential exfiltration.
external_assessments.assessment_summary: Mistral identifies compromised SDK releases, publication windows and a PyPI import-time payload that launched credential-harvesting code, while reporting no impact to Mistral's global infrastructure.
external_assessments.vigil_comparison_note: VIGIL treats the occurrence as a software-supply-chain package-provenance and release-integrity failure in ordinary-language governance terms, while retaining the Incident as unclassified under Failure Taxonomy 0.6.5 because no current selectable class precisely encodes malicious package-distribution substitution.

external_requirement_assessments.assessment_basis: Mistral removed the affected SDK releases after publication. This repaired the distribution path for those versions. The result covers release withdrawal. It does not establish restoration of developer credentials or attribute Mistral’s removal to Aikido’s detection.
external_requirement_assessments.identification_basis: Withdrawal of malicious AI client releases directly identifies repair of an unwanted state in the AI software distribution path.

external_requirement_assessments.assessment_basis: External detection and release removal are reported for the deployed AI client software. Mistral’s complete post-deployment monitoring procedures and their evaluation are not available.
Mistral removed the compromised SDK versions. The rate of implementing security recommendations and lessons across its AI software is not reported.
The SDK compromise and removal engage AI software security controls. Their regular assessment, metrics and subsequent updates are not reported.
The attack entered through the SDK supply chain. The explicit threat model, selected mitigations and their effectiveness tests are not available.

The provider’s distributed AI client SDK contained an import-time credential-harvesting payload. Developers receiving that component faced security risks through the normal import path. This AI software-distribution outcome is Not aligned. The advisory reports no impact to Mistral’s global infrastructure.
external_requirement_assessments.identification_basis: The AI provider’s compromised client SDK directly engages security of software used to access its AI systems.

external_requirement_assessments.assessment_basis: Malicious SDK releases were published and then removed. The regular verification of associated AI software security measures is not available. Publication alone does not establish which measure was assessed or compromised.
Aikido detected malicious releases and Mistral removed affected versions. Mistral’s monitoring of the robustness and effectiveness of its mitigation plans is not available.
The compromised releases engage review of AI software security guardrails. The cadence and substance of that review are not available.

The access-enforcement proposition requires approved logical-access authorisations to be enforced for information and system resources. The observed information operation was outside the approved boundary. Compromised SDK versions were published through a trusted release identity outside the normal release lineage. Publication changed the protected package contents. This is distinct from whether a victim later executed credential harvesting. This is a bounded retrospective comparison with the selected control proposition, not a claim of certification or an independently binding historical duty.
